reads.worst: The AES key sits in a 0600 file next to the store unless keyring is installed, so a copy of the Hermes folder opens it (disclosed in the README).

reads.best: Reads secrets via agent.secret_scope.get_secret rather than files, encrypts storage at rest, and ships 34 test files plus a dedicated evidence pack of safety checks.
reads.worst: The underlying idea (a structured people/contacts memory store) is a fairly direct application of a known pattern rather than something new for agents.

reads.best: Changes where Hermes runs, with the relay seed in Hermes's secret store, stripped from subprocesses, signed receipts and a real device+relay e2e test.
reads.worst: Heavy setup (pipx from git, HTTPS relay), relies on private Hermes internals, and witness mode blocks all device tools if any other plugin registers a pre_tool_call hook.

reads.best: A real proxy, SQLite recorder, drift checks and replay receipts give Hermes an evidence-based debugging loop, with usable UIs and concurrency and policy tests.
reads.worst: Replay can repeat side-effecting POSTs without a code-enforced human confirmation, and redaction or truncation means the stored request is not always an exact reproducible original.

reads.best: Its secret-store access, per-call human approval and payment-state re-fetch have focused tests and a polished demo.
reads.worst: It serves merchants with Zaprite accounts and depends on Zaprite for actual checkout and payment truth.

reads.best: Hooks, git snapshots, host-managed replay agents and a Desktop leaderboard address model selection using the user’s actual work.
reads.worst: The claimed confinement is unsafe: map_path accepts relative traversal as inside, and terminal handling only rewrites paths and workdir without containing commands.

reads.best: Fails closed throughout: the plugin rather than the voice agent compares the PIN, approvals are single-use and expire, one allowlisted number, daily cap, secrets come from Hermes's secret config, and there are tests.
reads.worst: Needs a paid CALL-E account and a phone call per approval, and the risky-tool guard is off by default and matches tool names only by regex.

reads.best: Careful secret handling (allowlisted names through scoped Hermes secrets, keys passed to workers over stdin), consent gating, and a full Desktop pane with native macOS capture and an overlay.
reads.worst: No tests ship ('runtime-only source release'), and the README itself calls it an early preview with unverified live answers and Windows path; the Meta ASR endpoint could not be verified.

reads.best: A plugin that builds, validates and grades Hermes plugins, with about 106 tests, secret-store keys in generated code and a designed Desktop page.
reads.worst: The README says templates can't carry injected code, but the raw title/description goes into a generated docstring that create() imports in-process, so a description with triple quotes can run code.

reads.best: Native hooks connect skill creation and later use to a local evidence trail, with reversible quarantine and regression tests for the main grading and recovery paths.
reads.worst: The error matcher treats "0 failed" as failure and the constraint matcher can flag "never git push main", so the default gate can quarantine valid skills.

reads.best: It integrates intent triage, skill indexing, memory retrieval and per-turn receipts into the Hermes context path.
reads.worst: The advertised 250 ms deadline is not enforced around synchronous model calls, so the default router can delay a turn.

reads.best: It uses Hermes middleware and persistent per-session state to make hint progression and teacher reporting more than prompt instructions, with adversarial and integration coverage.
reads.worst: Its answer screening is heuristic and fail-open, and CLI streaming can reveal unscreened output unless disabled; only CLI has been verified.

reads.best: Never unpickles: an opcode-level abstract interpreter reports exactly which callables an artifact would invoke, backed by 24 tests and a demo video.
reads.worst: The guard hook only spots load calls by regex in a fixed set of code tools, so loads phrased differently pass unchecked, and the idea overlaps existing picklescan-style scanners.

reads.best: Wave OS key read only via Hermes secret_scope, every add/update/remove/ask goes through the approval prompt and is refused in scheduled jobs, with 27 tests.
reads.worst: Serves a niche chain and store, starts a network re-check thread on load, and the README and dashboard docstring say nothing is paid or sent to Wave although ask_wave can spend TFUEL.

reads.best: Careful transport: key via the secret scope, redirects refused, no retries on billable calls, resumable video jobs, and a broad test suite.
reads.worst: Tied to one vendor's paid gateway, so few Hermes users would install it on day one.

reads.best: The event bridge covers subagents, context usage and human-input waits while limiting conversation excerpts and stripping provider keys from the child environment.
reads.worst: The renderer is outside this repository's pin, and send() writes unbounded tool arguments to a blocking stdin pipe before starting its timeout cleanup thread ([__init__.py](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/donlucasx/hermes-xscapes/3a12d11bdc4e7fd917b256014e7efcf4e79c9e3d/__init__.py)).

reads.best: Persistent research baselines and cron-aware acknowledgment prevent unattended checks from silently dismissing information needing a person.
reads.worst: Its usefulness depends on one external research service and narrow sector coverage, with some advertised themes still missing live readings.

reads.best: USSD-to-SMS handoff brings an agent to feature phones, and callback handling avoids duplicate agent turns.
reads.worst: There is no plugin README, and the webhook accepts unauthenticated callbacks when the optional secret is unset.

reads.best: Its human approval gate for writes is strict (mandatory approval policy, one-use lease, preview binding) and it has 100 tests; the key comes from Hermes's secret store.
reads.worst: The README admits that writes depend on unreleased Hermes core APIs, so on stable Hermes it is read- and preview-only; the docs are dense, with a 632-line validation log.

reads.best: It plugs search and extraction into Hermes’s existing web-provider interface and reads its API key through Hermes’s provider environment/secret lookup.
reads.worst: It depends on a paid third-party service and sends user queries and requested URLs to that service; the functionality is a backend option for familiar web tools.

reads.best: A polished keyless workflow with fixture tests, allowlisted bounded HTTP, useful fallbacks and explicit human booking/payment.
reads.worst: Its best-stay and best-ride choices lack live vacancy, room prices and ride quotes, relying on OSM tags and static regional fare assumptions.

reads.best: Verification is deterministic and auditable: the corpus ships with SHA-256 sums, the engine runs with a minimal environment and no credentials, and the adapter validates the engine's answer against a fixed contract with 50 tests.
reads.worst: A Linux-only, Spanish-language tool for Chilean lawyers with five Python dependencies, a slow first-call unpack, and a README section left as a placeholder to be completed by the maintainer.

reads.best: Destructive actions require typing the target, and a credential-free demo plus screenshot make it easy to try.
reads.worst: It is a cloud console with no tests and no agent tools, so it adds little that Hermes itself does.

reads.best: Ships substantial playable game engines, terminal graphics fallbacks, demos, and tests rather than a chat-only game prompt.
reads.worst: The /race path immediately executes model-written Python with the inherited process environment and no sandbox; a timeout does not constrain its file or network access.

reads.best: Its acquisition pipeline combines explicit policy choices, bounded extraction and staged writes that preserve existing outputs on failure.
reads.worst: Setup requires a manual dependency-install step, and the README explicitly leaves macOS/Linux and several external rendering runtimes unverified.

reads.best: The rewritten draft is never auto-applied; the user must click Apply, and the 6000-char limit is enforced in both the backend and the UI.
reads.worst: Functionally it is close to a prompt-based grammar check; the main plugin-only value is the Desktop toolbar button and REST route, not the proofreading logic itself.

reads.best: User-triggered tests cap each batch at 25 models and use scoped secrets, with status classification, redaction and request-limit tests.
reads.worst: Concurrent test requests share an unlocked JSON state file and fixed temporary filename, and malformed success responses can escape handling; live gateway integration is not established.

reads.best: Real per-card scheduling state and hooks that a prompt cannot keep.
reads.worst: A familiar Anki-style idea, and its tests sit in one file.

reads.best: Detailed engineering notes and mockups for a genuinely native-looking Win11 acrylic theme, including a terminal transparency fix.
reads.worst: No tests, and it works by overwriting the host's translucency store and force-losing xterm WebGL contexts, fragile hacks against Desktop internals for a cosmetic gain.

reads.best: Keys come only from Hermes's secret scope with redaction and a private-network guard, backed by about 249 parser/guard tests.
reads.worst: The README promises non-GET calls 'always require interactive approval' and fail under cron, but the only gate is a confirm flag the model sets itself and there is no unattended check; the README is marked work-in-progress with no setup.

reads.best: It is a substantial, well-documented theme that uses the Desktop theme API without network, storage, or agent-side privileges.
reads.worst: It has no tests and relies on many Desktop data-slot and class selectors that can silently break as the host UI changes.

reads.best: Clear README on data leaving the machine, pinned MCP version and untrusted trust flag.
reads.worst: Plugin is only a manifest, mcp.json and skill; real logic and a paid key live in an external service.

reads.best: It separates read-only market queries from prepare-action links, labels the MCP server untrusted, and keeps signing in the user's own wallet.
reads.worst: Live tool behavior is supplied by kyte.sh rather than the pinned repository, and the feature depends on an external finance service with no local tests or implementation to inspect.

reads.best: A careful permission model: only owner slash commands can approve, and test runs use bwrap --unshare-all with cap-drop, rlimits and a deadline, with 102 tests.
reads.worst: Its tagline overstates the code (no merge; the daily wake only returns a cron request), it adds up to about 3 KB to every LLM call, and its jargon-heavy README has no screenshots or UI.

reads.best: Read-only, OAuth through a pinned mcp-remote version, marked 'untrusted', with a clear README on what data leaves and where.
reads.worst: No code of its own: a config pointing at a vendor's hosted MCP server that needs a paid Audionotes account, so its value rests entirely on that service.

reads.best: Read-only local schema and chain checks offer concrete verification while explicitly distinguishing internal consistency from independent proof.
reads.worst: The shipped test harness looks for a nonexistent nested asin-hhc-proof-of-pay package, and chain consistency cannot independently establish that the work or payment occurred.

reads.best: Claims can become contested or suspect as reviews and withdrawn ancestors change the graph, making shared knowledge revisable.
reads.worst: The client reads read_token and write_token directly from config.yaml or os.environ rather than Hermes’s secret scope, violating the catalog credential rule.

reads.best: The connector explicitly keeps remote tools untrusted and documents the native Hermes OAuth workaround, spending boundaries and limited read-only qualification.
reads.worst: The pinned tree contains only connector manifests and skills, so creative execution and service-side approval claims cannot be inspected, and sign-in requires manual native configuration.

reads.best: The small toolset directly supports durable project context and checkpoint retrieval without external services or credentials.
reads.worst: The implementation is a conventional CRUD tracker with limited surfaced error handling and relatively basic documentation and tests.

reads.best: The password secret is resolved through Hermes's secret_scope first before falling back to a plain env var, matching the catalog's secret-handling expectations.
reads.worst: Calling fortograph_redact/unredact uploads the user's image to a remote third-party server immediately with no approval gate, and the only verification is a single manual end-to-end script requiring live network access, not an automated test suite.

reads.best: Marks the server untrusted so Hermes asks before every write, uses OAuth through Hermes with no keys in the package, and the skill teaches find-before-change and confirm-before-delete.
reads.worst: The whole plugin is a two-line mcp.json and a skill for a vendor's existing MCP server, and the README is the generic multi-client Superlist MCP page rather than a Hermes one.

reads.best: Browser sign-in with a state check, and Cognito tokens cached in a 0600 file per tenant.
reads.worst: Its own VERIFICATION.md says `hermes plugins validate` fails and it must not be called install-ready; the password comes from a plain env var rather than Hermes's secret store; prod links use a hard-coded interview-test domain; and an unknown email falls back to recruiter@hireko.ai.

reads.best: Gives agents a public, read-only eldercare directory and cost calculator with no account needed.
reads.worst: The package is only a remote MCP URL and a 24-line skill. All the logic is on a company server that can't be reviewed, and the README is mostly product marketing.

reads.best: No code of its own and no stored credential: Hermes keeps the OAuth token, and the README spells out what order data is sent.
reads.worst: A thin config for a commercial rewards service: it asks the agent to send the user's Amazon order items and prices to a third party, its tools run without approval under default trust, and the pull request is still open.

reads.best: The package explicitly marks the remote server untrusted and clearly discloses credit use, browser sign-in and user-confirmed publishing.
reads.worst: The pinned tree contains only configuration and docs, leaving server behavior and tests unreviewable, while OAuth tokens are stored by mcp-remote outside Hermes.

reads.best: Marks the server untrusted and takes the key from an env variable, with a skill that asks before writes.
reads.worst: About three tiny files, no README, tests or setup docs; works only with a paid third-party service.

reads.best: The [MIDI backend](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/james-see/midi-bridge/5c94d270116454795f644e2118f1f42e057da808/midi_utils.py) opens local virtual or existing ports, giving Hermes a concrete way to play a user's instruments.
reads.worst: The [sequence player](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/james-see/midi-bridge/5c94d270116454795f644e2118f1f42e057da808/pattern_player.py) sleeps each absolute start time plus each preceding note duration, so timing drifts and notes cannot overlap.

reads.best: The small package uses profile secrets and marks its write-capable remote MCP server untrusted.
reads.worst: The pinned repository contains only a skill and remote configuration, with no server implementation or tests to assess the advertised reporting behavior.

reads.best: Careful skill with ask-before-each-step rules and an MCP test.
reads.worst: It is essentially a skill and static templates, not a Hermes plugin that changes what Hermes can do.

reads.best: The concise workflow preserves unknown dates, flags duplicate registrations and formula cells, and keeps imports under user control.
reads.worst: It contains only instructions and metadata, with no executable CSV validator, Hermes-specific tool, or live Fleetkeep integration.
